paragraphs.title: A Promise of Revelation and Jerusalem's Restoration

answers: In the temple
In the court of the prison
At the city gate
easy.explanation: Jeremiah was shut up in the court of the prison.
easy.q: Where was Jeremiah when the word of the Lord came unto him?

answers: Answer him and show him great and mighty things
Send him to fight the Chaldeans
Remove him from Jerusalem
easy.explanation: The Lord promised to answer Jeremiah and show him things he did not know.
easy.q: What did the Lord promise to do when Jeremiah called unto Him?

answers: A new wall
A great army
Health and cure
easy.explanation: The Lord promised to bring health and cure and to reveal peace and truth.
easy.q: What did the Lord promise to bring to the city?

answers: Destruction will be followed by healing and restoration
The destruction will continue forever
The city will leave the land
medium.explanation: Although the city faced siege and destruction, the Lord promised healing, peace, and restoration.
medium.q: What contrast is shown between the city's condition and the Lord's promise?

answers: Tall buildings
Wonderful things not yet known to Jeremiah
Only fortified cities
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to great and hidden matters that Jeremiah did not know.
medium.q: What does the phrase “great and mighty things” refer to?

answers: Only new cities would be built
They would make war upon the nations
They would be cleansed, forgiven, and restored
medium.explanation: The Lord promised to return the captives, cleanse their iniquity, and pardon their sins.
medium.q: What would happen when Judah and Israel were restored?

answers: They would hear of it and fear and tremble
They would leave their own lands
They would destroy Jerusalem again
challenge.explanation: The nations would hear of the goodness and prosperity the Lord gave Jerusalem and would fear and tremble.
challenge.q: How would the nations respond to Jerusalem's restoration?

answers: Kings are contrasted with priests
Imprisonment, siege, and destruction are contrasted with healing, forgiveness, and peace
Day is contrasted with night
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from the city's ruined condition to promised healing, pardon, and renewal.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in this passage?

answers: Restoration is unrelated to the people's conduct
The city will be saved by military strength
Restoration includes repaired fellowship between the Lord and His people
challenge.explanation: Cleansing and pardon show that the restoration is spiritual as well as national.
challenge.q: What does the mention of both sin and pardon show about restoration?

paragraphs.title: The Return of Life, Joy, and Pasture

answers: The voice of joy and gladness
Only the sounds of war
Only the sound of weeping
easy.explanation: The passage says that the voice of joy and the voice of gladness would be heard again.
easy.q: What sounds would again be heard in places that had been desolate?

answers: Soldiers and kings
The bridegroom and the bride
Prophets only
easy.explanation: The voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride are named.
easy.q: Whose voices are specifically mentioned in the passage?

answers: The sacrifice of praise
Building stones
Hidden flocks
easy.explanation: They would bring the sacrifice of praise into the house of the Lord.
easy.q: What would people bring into the house of the Lord?

answers: They would remain without man and beast
They would become battlefields
They would again contain people, joy, shepherds, and flocks
medium.explanation: Desolate places would be restored with joyful people, shepherds, and flocks.
medium.q: What change would take place in the desolate cities?

answers: A dwelling place
A weapon of war
A city gate
medium.explanation: An habitation is a place where shepherds and their flocks dwell.
medium.q: In the phrase “an habitation of shepherds,” what does “habitation” mean?

answers: Both express the return of communal life and joy
Both describe punishment
Both prepare for war
medium.explanation: The wedding and worship voices show that ordinary and religious life have returned.
medium.q: How are wedding voices and Temple worship related in this passage?

answers: They show that restoration would reach many regions
They identify only the location of the Temple
They prove that every city had been destroyed
challenge.explanation: The list shows the broad extent of renewed life and pasture throughout the land.
challenge.q: Why are the mountains, valleys, south, Benjamin, Jerusalem, and Judah mentioned?

answers: A change from private life to royal rule
A change from emptiness to renewed community life
A change from worship to shepherding
challenge.explanation: Wedding voices symbolize the renewal of families and community life.
challenge.q: What does the change from desolation to the voice of the bride and bridegroom symbolize?

answers: Order, pasture, and productive life have returned
The flocks are being sent to fight an enemy
The cities remain in ruins
challenge.explanation: Counted flocks and active shepherds show that the land is inhabited and functioning again.
challenge.q: What does the flocks passing under the hands of the one who telleth them indicate?

paragraphs.title: A Righteous Shoot for the House of David

answers: David
The kings of Canaan
The shepherds
easy.explanation: The Branch of righteousness would grow up unto David.
easy.q: For whom would the Lord cause the Branch of righteousness to grow?

answers: Build a fleet of ships
Execute judgment and righteousness in the land
Destroy Jerusalem
easy.explanation: The ruler would execute judgment and righteousness in the land.
easy.q: What would the promised ruler do?

answers: Judah would be saved and Jerusalem would dwell safely
Both would remain desolate
They would belong to the Chaldeans
easy.explanation: The passage promises salvation for Judah and safety for Jerusalem.
easy.q: What would happen to Judah and Jerusalem in those days?

answers: The connection between righteous rule and Jerusalem's security
The name of a particular priest
The wall around the city
medium.explanation: The name reflects the promised righteousness connected with the ruler and the safety of Jerusalem.
medium.q: What does the name “The Lord our righteousness” emphasize?

answers: David's royal line and the service of the priests and Levites
The rule of the Chaldeans and Egyptians
The work of shepherds and merchants
medium.explanation: The Lord promises a continuing ruler from David and priests and Levites to offer sacrifices.
medium.q: Which two continuing ministries are promised in this passage?

answers: The ruler will execute judgment and righteousness in the land
The Branch will become a physical wall
Jerusalem will have no inhabitants
medium.explanation: The promised ruler's righteous government is linked with Judah's salvation and Jerusalem's security.
medium.q: Why is Jerusalem's safety connected with the righteous Branch?

answers: The renewed growth of just Davidic leadership
Only agricultural growth
The end of the priests' service
challenge.explanation: The Branch is a picture of a new ruler from David who will govern justly.
challenge.q: What does the “Branch of righteousness” symbolize?

answers: Restoration includes political leadership and holy service
The priesthood will replace the monarchy
The monarchy will abolish Temple worship
challenge.explanation: The passage preserves both David's royal line and the ministry of the priests and Levites.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the mention of both the monarchy and the priesthood?

answers: Both are connected with righteousness
Both are connected with pasture
Both are connected with destruction
challenge.explanation: The ruler will execute righteousness, and Jerusalem will be called “The Lord our righteousness.”
challenge.q: What connection exists between the promised ruler and Jerusalem's name?

paragraphs.title: The Unbreakable Covenant with David and the Levites

answers: The order of day and night
The changing seasons
The speed of an army
easy.explanation: The Lord refers to His covenant of the day and His covenant of the night.
easy.q: What does the Lord use to illustrate the stability of His covenant?

answers: David and the Levites
The Chaldeans and Egyptians
The shepherds and merchants
easy.explanation: The covenant includes David and the Levites, His ministers.
easy.q: With whom does the Lord promise to maintain His covenant?

answers: Only grains of desert sand
The host of heaven and the sand of the sea
The number of Judah's cities
easy.explanation: The Lord promised to multiply them like the host of heaven and the sand of the sea.
easy.q: What would the seed of David and the Levites become like in number?

answers: The appointed order of day and night cannot be broken
The people demanded it
The priests won a war
medium.explanation: The covenant is presented as firm as the continuing order of day and night.
medium.q: What reason does the Lord give for the certainty of His covenant?

answers: The covenant could be ended
The covenant could not be built
The covenant could not be counted
medium.explanation: The phrase describes the covenant as breakable only if the established order of day and night could first be broken.
medium.q: What does “may also my covenant be broken” mean in context?

answers: It shows lasting and abundant continuation
It shows that the people will disappear
It removes the Levites from service
medium.explanation: The comparisons with heaven's host and sea sand emphasize enduring multiplication.
medium.q: How does the promise of numerous descendants strengthen the covenant?

answers: If the created order remains, the covenant will also remain
If the people sin, every promise ends
If Jerusalem is desolate, it has no future
challenge.explanation: The Lord uses the unchanging order of day and night to support the certainty of His covenant.
challenge.q: What argument is used in these verses?

answers: They represent continuing royal leadership and continuing worship
They are presented as two enemies
They describe the division of the land
challenge.explanation: The covenant includes both the Davidic throne and the priestly ministry.
challenge.q: Why are David and the Levites both mentioned?

answers: A number too great to count
The borders of the land
The destruction of the Temple
challenge.explanation: Both images express an immeasurably large and enduring number.
challenge.q: What is emphasized by the comparison with the host of heaven and the sand of the sea?

paragraphs.title: Rejecting the People's Claim and Restoring the Tribes

answers: The Lord had chosen them again
The Lord had cast them off
They had willingly left the land
easy.explanation: The people said that the Lord had cast off the two families He had chosen.
easy.q: What did the people say about the two families chosen by the Lord?

answers: Israel was no more a nation before the Lord
Israel had become greater than before
Jerusalem had become a trading city
easy.explanation: They claimed that Israel should be no more a nation before the Lord.
easy.q: What other claim did the people make about Israel?

answers: Leave the people in captivity
Cause their captivity to return and have mercy on them
Replace them with another people
easy.explanation: The Lord promised to restore their captivity and show them mercy.
easy.q: What did the Lord promise to do at the end of the passage?

answers: He points again to His covenant with day and night
He declares that there is no covenant
He commands the people to make war
medium.explanation: The Lord argues that as His ordinances of heaven and earth remain, His covenant also remains.
medium.q: How does the Lord answer the people's claim?

answers: Chosen them
Rejected or abandoned them
Blessed them
medium.explanation: To cast off means to reject or abandon, which is the claim the Lord rejects.
medium.q: In the phrase “he hath even cast them off,” what does “cast them off” mean?

answers: Jacob, David, and the Levites
Moses, Aaron, and Joshua only
Pharaoh and the king of Assyria
medium.explanation: The passage mentions the seed of Jacob, David, and the Levites.
medium.q: Which people and lines are named to support the promise?

answers: They claim rejection, while He answers with covenant, restoration, and mercy
They ask for war, while He promises peace with an enemy
They ask for a king, while He abolishes the monarchy
challenge.explanation: The Lord rejects the idea of abandonment and confirms His continuing covenant and compassion.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between the people's claim and the Lord's response?

answers: They represent the continuity of the people, the royal line, and holy service
They identify three regions of the land
They distinguish Israel from its enemies
challenge.explanation: Together they represent Israel's national, royal, and priestly continuity.
challenge.q: Why are Jacob, David, and the Levites mentioned together?

answers: Restoration is not merely political but also an act of compassion
The people will remain without hope
The priesthood will be abolished
challenge.explanation: The restoration is joined with mercy, showing the Lord's gracious concern for His people.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the closing words “and have mercy on them”?
